### D432 — The Model carries `signed`, `reason` and `location`; where the new nodes stand; a signature's picture is no figure (P8.3; SPEC 10.7, 10.6; D053, D318, D376)
**Decision**: `fk-signed` (99, a boolean) and `fk-location` (100) are new Model attributes and `fk-reason` (51, the ledger's) is a seal's too: JSON (`signed`, `reason`, `location` after `color`), HTML (`data-emon-signed`, `data-emon-reason`, `data-emon-location` on the seal's `<figure>`) and `schema/emon-1.json` have them; only a digital signature has them. D318 places a seal node before the first block that starts below its TOP when it overlaps no block: a signature field is a widget as tall as two lines of text with its label beside it, so by its top the field came BEFORE its own label (`Approved by`): `sm-ref-y` uses a digital signature field's BOTTOM, so the label whose line starts inside its height comes first. And a signature, initials or a digital signature that overlaps no block is placed AFTER the last top-level block of its page that starts above its reference y (`sm-last-above`), where D318 put it before the first block that starts below it, a LATER page's too: the initials at the foot of page 1 were the first node of page 2's section. D318's rule stays for seals and stamps (nothing of theirs changes). **A signature's picture is no figure**: P8.1 made the JPEG of a raster signature a `figure` of kind `photo` and took the typed name under it and the label above it for its `labels`, so two words of the page's own text left the body; `fc-signature-over` (`kin/figclass.kin`; `fc-stage` takes the `sl` arena now) rejects an image region that is at most four times the box of a signature or initials read from pixels and has half of itself under it (a signature inside a photograph is not this). Raster SEALS (P8.2) still have their figure beside them, as they did: a measure of the maintainer's to take. **Alternatives**: its centre; leaving D318 as it was and the reader taking a label's field before it; suppressing the figure at `sm-write` (the copy would skip a node and its subtree).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D433 — The metrics, the scoreboard, and what was measured (P8.3; D079, D209, D418)
**Decision**: the scorer counts, for every document that has a gold, `sig` and `init` (the gold's seal nodes of the subkind, the predicted ones, and as many true positives as the two lists share by count: a node has no box in the gold), the typed `name` of every gold signature that has one (a predicted signature not yet taken has the same letters and digits) and a digital signature as right when a predicted one not yet taken agrees on `name`, `date`, `reason`, `location` and `signed`: `seal-sig-p/r/f1`, `seal-init-p/r/f1`, `sig-name-acc`, `digsig-acc`. `emon-sigs` is a FIXTURE SET (as `emon-figures`): the four fixtures of `test/signatures`, their gold `gold/ID.gold.json` (written by the generator), the Rust Engine REPLAYING `test/signatures/replay/ID` (`tools/accuracy/predict-emon-sigs.sh`); 150 metrics in `pdf/all` and `pdf/seals`, every signature, initials and digital-signature metric 1.0, `cer` 0.0, `bow-f1` 1.0, `block-seal-p/r` 1.0, `conf-ece-seal` 0.262 (uncalibrated: `bb calibration --refit` at the merge, once `test/signatures` is among its documents). New metrics recorded in two existing entries: `emon-sealpx` (`scan-ovl/seals`: `seal-sig-p` 1.0, `seal-sig-r` 0.25, `sig-name-acc` 1.0, and `block-seal-r` 0.3636 -> 0.4545, `block-seal-f1` 0.5333 -> 0.625, `conf-brier-seal` 0.325 -> 0.292), `emon-fusion` (`pdf/seals`: `seal-sig-p/r` 1.0, `sig-name-acc` 1.0; the `seal` calibration metrics improved). No value was lowered.
**Measured** (BEFORE is the P8.2 branch built and replaying the same transcripts of `test/signatures`): signatures 0 of 3 found -> 3 of 3 (precision and recall 1.00), typed names 0 of 3 -> 3 of 3, initials 0 of 2 -> 2 of 2, digital-signature fields 0 of 3 -> 3 of 3 (a conversion with no OCR port writes the same three), body words lost 3 -> 0 (the raster signature's picture was a `figure`, `photo`, and `Seller` and `Jordan Lee` its labels), words in the body that are not the page's 0 -> 0 (the strokes OCR read as letters stay out of it); `sig-negatives` (a doodle over a paragraph, a rule with a typed name and no ink, a chart's line standing on its axes, a raster scribble, a `Signature:` label with nothing) has no node. The scan (`sig-scan`: 150 dpi, noise, blur, JPEG 60, a third of a degree turned): the signature, its name and all 55 words. Gates: `bb sigs`, `bb seals` (the two signature fixtures' digests re-recorded: the node has its `name` now), `bb fusion` (160 checks, one digest re-recorded: `sig-over-name`'s name), `bb sealpx` (`ovl-sig-over-name`'s digest: the signature), `bb retarget` (45 checks, nothing changed), `bb accuracy` (`emon`: 3246 metrics, none lower).
**Why the corpus's scanned overlays are not found**: the `scan-ovl` documents lay a generated signature over the page at a place with no rule under it (the gold says `signature`; nothing on the page does): three of the four gold signatures of `stamp-seal`, `seal-over-text` and `sig-over-name`. A raster cue that is not a rule (a colon token or a hint word read by OCR as such) would find some; the first pass does not read a pen's neighbours as such words reliably, so it was not built (D430). **Not measured**: initials on a real corpus (the corpus has none), a handwriting corpus (none is committed; every threshold is a first value: P10.1), mapo80 (stamps, no signatures), a signature file in the wild (the CMS of `sig-digital` is openssl's: an Adobe or a PAdES one has more certificates and `SignerInfo` first, and the second `commonName` of the bytes is then a chain's, not the signer's: D426).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D434 — One options grammar, parsed by kin into `Cfg`; the tables of limits and settings are kin's (P10.10; D396 items 1 and 5, D406)
**Decision**: (1) `emon.config` owns the `key=value` text an embedder says a conversion is asked to do in: lines separated by LF (a CR before it is dropped), empty lines nothing, split at the first `=`, the last line that sets a key wins except `limit.NAME` and `producer.NAME`, which are lists. Keys: `locale ocr furniture assets asset-dpi asset-pixels asset-bytes assets-bytes asset-signatures keep-evidence ocr-scope max-rounds fetch-rounds record js-ocr chunk limit.NAME producer.NAME`. The key table (shape, range, name) and the table of enum words (key, code, spelling) are `defdata`; the sentence of every refusal (`ocr is always, auto or never` is written from the table; `asset-dpi wants a number, not "x"`; `unknown option K`; `no limit named N`) is kin's. `cf-parse` fills a `Cfg` (the defaults are `cf-defaults`; `Cfg` gained `chunk maxr fetchr rec jsocr num lims prod msg`) and answers 0, or 1 with the sentence in `msg`; `cf-is-key` tells a driver whether `--name=` is kin's. (2) `emon.limits` (pure: it refers no port form, so Go's `port` package can import it, D405) holds the limit table (kind = row, name, default, range 0..2^31-1) and the setting table (`ocr-mode`, `tasks`). A host's `limit-of` is override, then `EMON_LIMIT_<NAME>`, then kin's default; `setting-of` the same from kin's setting table; `limit_spec`/`setting_spec` and their copies in Go, Java and C# are deleted. The environment name is the table's name in capitals with `_` for `-`. (3) The idiomatic typed structs stay: Rust `Options`/`Config`, Go `Options`/`Config` are filled from the `Cfg` by `parse_options`/`ParseOptions` (returning a `Parsed` with the Options, the Config, `record`, `js-ocr` and the producer pairs), and `Options::default()`/`Config::default()` are the parse of the empty text, so no default is typed in a host. The wasm binding and both drivers call it; a driver collects every `--key=value` flag kin knows into a text and parses it once (`--limit.pages=5` is new for free). The host-only flags (`--out`, `--record=DIR`, `--source`, `--async`, ...) are matched first. (4) Rust `Options` -> `Cfg` (`cfg_of`) stays the direct field copy: the typed path needs no text. (5) Behaviour changes, all refusals of nonsense that used to be accepted: `asset-signatures` is `on` or `off` in the browser binding too (anything else was `off`); `chunk` is at least 1 (`--chunk=0`); a limit is at least 0; a number is an i32 without `-2147483648`; `limit.NAME` of a name not in the table and an unknown key stay refused as before. The wasm module's `chunk` argument still decides the chunk size (the JS source decides it, not the options).
**Why**: the wasm binding and each driver parsed the same options with a hand-written list that had already drifted (the driver took `--asset-signatures` strictly, the binding did not; the binding had `limit.` and the loop's bounds, the drivers had neither), and the C binding and the pod would have been a third and fourth copy; a limit's name, default and range were a table in four spellings.
**Alternatives**: building `Cfg` from `Options` by writing the text and re-parsing (a round trip per conversion for no new check; the typed fields are already validated by their types); a `setting.NAME` key for the settings (no source reads a setting through anything but the environment yet).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D435 — A limit breach unwinds with a typed payload (kind, limit, actual) on every host, caught by its type (P10.10; D406, D396 item 3)
**Decision**: `limit-breach` still never returns, and what it raises is a value of a type, not a sentence: Rust `std::panic::panic_any(port::LimitBreach { kind, limit, actual })`, Go `panic(&port.Breach{...})`, Java `throw new Port.Breach(...)` and C# `throw new Port.Breach(...)` (both exceptions). `limit` is the bound in force when it was raised (the override, the environment or the default), `actual` what the input reached. A host catches it by its TYPE (`downcast_ref::<LimitBreach>()`, a type assertion, `catch (Port.Breach)`), and the name of the limit is kin's table's (`port::limit_name`, `port.LimitName`, `Port.limitName`/`LimitName`: the host spells the name out of `emon.limits`' code points). The type has a message (`Display`/`Error()`/`getMessage()`) for a person, with the old words; nothing reads it. `lb-parse` and its helpers are deleted from `emon.planloop`, with Rust's `panic_error` and Go's `panicError` message parse (they are now `panic_error(Box<dyn Any>)`/`panicError(any)`); a panic that only says a limit's words is `internal`. Go's `planError` no longer scans `"the limit is %d and this run reached %d"`: `port.PlanError` carries `Limited`, `Limit` and `Actual` from the plan context (`err-limit`, `err-actual`). The fuzz probes (Rust, Go, Java, C#) write `LIMIT-<name>` for the payload, and `tools/fuzz/fuzz.clj` no longer rewrites `PANIC the ... limit is` lines. **Not `:throws`**: kin's `^:throws` tags make a result carry an error to the caller, and every kin function that reads a limit would have to return that tag; a breach unwinds from deep inside a unit and is caught where the host already catches panics, so a typed host payload is the smaller change, and kin still sees nothing but `limit-breach`, which never returns. The browser binding builds with `panic=unwind`, so the payload reaches its guard as on a native host.
**Why**: four hosts parsed one English sentence back into a name; the sentence was a contract nobody wrote down, and the name is a table kin owns.
**Alternatives**: a kin-visible latched status checked after each stage (changes every limit-reading function's result and the order of every stage's checks); a message prefix of a fixed shape (still a parse).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D436 — Limit overrides stay scoped by platform, and that difference is documented (P10.10; D396 item 1)
**Decision**: the table of limits is shared; the scope of an override is not. Rust: a thread-local table (`port::with_limits`), installed for one conversion on the calling thread, so conversions with different bounds run side by side. Go: a process-wide table behind a `sync.RWMutex` (`port.WithLimits`): a conversion with overrides takes the lock exclusively and runs ALONE in the process, one without overrides takes it shared and never sees one (Go has no goroutine-local state). Java and C# (when their Engines merge): process-wide behind a lock, as Go, or a `ThreadLocal`/`AsyncLocal` where the host runs a conversion on one thread; their `Port` has no override yet. In every host the environment `EMON_LIMIT_<NAME>` is below an override and above kin's default. An embedder that needs per-conversion bounds in parallel on Go, Java or C# runs separate processes or serialises; the browser binding is one thread. This is the platform's difference to be seen, not unified: a thread-local in Go would need goroutine identity, and a lock in Rust would serialise conversions that are independent.
**Why**: P10.10 asked that scoping stay per platform and be written down.
**Alternatives**: one process-wide scope everywhere (loses Rust's parallel conversions with different bounds); passing the bounds as a context argument into every unit (a `Cfg` field read by `limit-of` would change the signature of the form on four hosts and every unit that reads a limit).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D437 — What changed for an embedder, for Java and C#, and what P10.10 leaves (P10.10; D434-D436)
**Decision**: Rust: new `Parsed`, `parse_options`, `is_option_key` at the crate root; `Options::default()`/`Config::default()` are kin's parse of the empty text; `port::LimitBreach` is the panic payload of a breach, `port::limit_name` the table's name; the `Cfg` of `emon.enctx` has nine more fields, so a host that builds one by field must keep `Cfg::new()`. Go: `Parsed`, `ParseOptions`, `IsOptionKey`, `DefaultOptions`/`DefaultConfig` from kin; `port.Breach`, `port.LimitName`; `port.PlanError` gains `Limited`, `Limit`, `Actual`; `host/go/port` imports `emon/limits` (pure). Java and C# are not on main: their `Port` already throws `Port.Breach` and reads `Limits` here (`bb check` and `bb unit` compile and run it), and when their Engines merge they replace their English-message parse with a catch of `Port.Breach` by type, replace `Options` fields with `Config`/`Parsed` (Java's `ocrBornDigital` and its siblings are the drift this ends) and take their `Cfg` from the parse. Left: the settings (`OCR_MODE`, `TASKS`) have no key in the grammar because no source reads one other than through the environment; the C binding and the pod are later items, and take `cf-parse` as it is.
**Why**: the host surface changed in four places; recording who adopts what keeps the Java and C# merges mechanical.
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D438 — The transcript is `emon.transcript`; the host keeps files and bitmaps (P10.9; D396, D404, D405, D214, SPEC 13)
**Decision**: (1) `kin/transcriptctx.kin` declares `Tr`, what one transcript holds (the inputs, the producer in file order, the entries back to back, the bitmap names a file gave, the replay map, the sentence of the error a read stopped on); `kin/transcript.kin` is the module. `tr-write` writes `transcript.edn` to a `Text`: FORMAT VERSION 1, byte for byte what the hosts wrote (the key order, the spaces, `:kind :unknown` for a kind the table does not have, `:bitmap` named from the entry's place `bitmap-0000.png`, the producer escaped: a backslash is `/`, a double quote `'`). `tr-read` reads it from a Blob into the cells of `Tr`: the whole file is checked to be UTF-8 and well-formed EDN first, then read for what a transcript is, with the order of the checks and the first-of-a-repeated-key rule the hosts had. (2) The replay map is `idx`, keyed by the WHOLE request record (`tr-index`, `tr-find`, `tr-take`; of two entries of one request the later is the map's, the earlier is never asked for, as before); `tr-unused` and `tr-unused-msg` count the entries a replay never asked for, and `tr-miss-msg`, `tr-check-inputs` say the sentences of `transcript-miss` and of a replay given other inputs. (3) The names: `tk` (render, decode, ocr, crop, decode-img; `bytes` is the loop's own and is not recorded), `tf` (the keys of the file) and `tb` (the reasons of `transcript-bad`, spelled as the sentence the hosts always said), all `defenum`s; the reader finds a name by `tk-find` and `tf-find`, so a name is spelled once (D439). (4) The host keeps file I/O, the bitmaps and `png_decode` (until P10.11's transcript PNG reader), and its in-memory `Transcript` (`inputs`, `entries` with their bitmaps, `producer`): `to_files` and `from_files` build a `Tr` and call kin, the `Replayer` is a `Tr` indexed plus the entries' bitmaps. (5) The JavaScript SDK holds no EDN and no kind name: it passes the files the wasm binding (Rust's `plan.rs` over kin) writes and reads, so it calls kin through the module.
**Why**: D396 (the transcript is observable behaviour: its writer, reader, escaping and replay map were written four times; Java needed an ordered-map `producerInOrder` workaround for a producer that must be written back in the order read, and Go read the producer by scanning the text a second time).
**Alternatives**: keeping the host `Transcript` as kin's data (the tests and drivers read `entries[i].req`, `.bitmap`; a bitmap is a host object) -- the entries stay host-side, and kin is handed a copy to write or index; a reader that builds a tree (kin cannot allocate one), so the file is read twice, once for syntax and once for structure.
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D439 — `defenum ^:parse` adds `nm-find`: emon vocabulary, a gap fixed (P10.9; D028, D039)
**Decision**: `(defenum ^:pub ^:parse tk [...])` also defines `tk-find`, which reads a spelling out of a span of a Blob (`from`, `to`) and answers its code, or -1: a flat run of byte comparisons written from the same rows as `tk-emit-name`. Nothing else changes: an enum without `^:parse` generates what it did (`bb emit` rewrote no committed file but the new ones). The generator refuses a row named `nm-find`.
**Why**: `emon.lang` has no string tag on purpose (D028), so a reader could not compare a keyword with a name, and a second spelling in a `case` of bytes beside the writer's is the drift this ticket removes.
**Alternatives**: a hand-written finder per table (a second spelling); a hash of the span (collides).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D440 — Go: the transcript is `planrun`'s, and `port` names no error (P10.9; D405, D408)
**Decision**: `Transcript`, `File` (was `PlanFile`), `TranscriptFile`, `TranscriptFromFiles`, `Replayer` and `NewReplayer` moved from `host/go/port/plan.go` to `host/go/planrun/transcript.go` (the generated `transcript` imports `port`); `port` keeps `PlanEntry`, the fulfillers, the requests and answers and the PNG reader. `port` held its own literals of `fulfil-failed`, `transcript-bad` and `transcript-miss`: now a port returns `*port.FulfilError` (render.go), `planrun.Machine.Fulfil` makes it the loop's `fulfil-failed` from kin's `pe`, and `planrun.Bad`, `planrun.FulfilFailed` make the others; `engine.go` and the drivers use them. `planrun.Replayer.Done()` is the end-of-run check and replaces `Unused() != 0` and its hand-made `transcript-bad` at every call site (the Engines and the drivers, on both hosts). Rust: `Replayer::unused` takes `&mut self` (kin's map is a context) and `Replayer::check_done` is the same check. D408 stands: `port/render.go` still reads a render request by offsets it holds (the request records did not move).
**Why**: D405; D408 named these literals as P10.9's.
**Alternatives**: a hook in `port` for kin's names (a global set by an init, as `PngEncoder` is); only `fulfil-failed` is the port's, and it is no more than a type.

### D441 — What changed for an embedder, for a file, and for Java and C# (P10.9; D438-D440)
**Decision**: Files: none (the committed transcripts are unchanged: the law reads every one and writes it again). A reader is stricter or looser in these ways only, all of them on files the format never wrote: a file that is not UTF-8 is `transcript-bad` on Go too (it was read as U+FFFD); an integer is an I32 (the hosts truncated an i64 or failed); a document nested more than 64 deep is refused (`nested too deeply`; it was a stack overflow); the sentence of a syntax error carries a byte offset where Rust's carried a character index and Go's the character, and the sentences of `transcript-miss` and the unused count are one text (Rust printed `{:?}` of the record, Go the record with spaces); Go's `an input needs :index and :length` is two sentences like Rust's. Rust: `Replayer::unused(&mut self)`, `Replayer::check_done`, `Transcript::check_inputs` unchanged in signature; Go: `emon.Transcript = planrun.Transcript`, `planrun.TranscriptFromFiles`, `planrun.NewReplayer`, `File` for `PlanFile`, `Replayer.Done()`. Java and C# (branches `worktree-agent-a92de59fd1d1107a8` and `worktree-agent-ac9333ffec3452818`) adopt `emon.transcript` when they merge: build a `Tr` (`TrAddInput`, `TrAddProducer`, `TrAddEntry`) and `TrWrite`, or `TrRead` a Blob and read the entries by `TrE*` (the producer in file order by `TrP*`, which deletes Java's `producerInOrder`), index with `TrIndex` and answer a request by `TrTake`; their PNG codecs stay theirs.
**Why**: the format is kin's, so a host cannot differ; the sentences are kin's too.

### D442 — The laws, and the list of transcripts they read (P10.9; D044, D438)
**Decision**: `kin/transcripttest.kin` holds the names (a kind, a key and a reason are spelled once and found again; the kinds are `emon.plan`'s), the file as version 1 writes it, the places of the bitmaps (`bitmap-0000.png` ... `bitmap-12345.png`), the escaping edge cases (a backslash, a quote, only escapes, an empty value, a non-ASCII value as UTF-8, a backslash escape in the file read back and written escaped), what a reader refuses and the sentence it says (some sixty refusals, one for every reason, each with the byte offset where the sentence has one), the replay map (whole-record keys, a shorter or longer record, an offset into cells, nothing before `tr-index`, an empty transcript, two entries of one request, 1 to 1000 entries each found by its own record and its neighbour missed, cells near the ends of an I32) and the entries nobody asked for. One law reads EVERY transcript committed under `test/` (`test/transcript/manifest.txt`, one path a line) and checks that it reads, writes the same bytes, and that every entry is found by its own request. kin lists no directory, so `tools/transcript_manifest.clj --check` (called by `bb unit`) holds the list to the tree.
**Why**: the move is a pure move, and "every committed transcript" is a claim about the tree.

### D444 — Image input: kin validators in front of the platform decoders; the host reads the whole file and the library is shown what kin kept (P10.11; D396(4), D188-D190, D389)
**Decision**: `emon.pngcheck` (`pc-check`) and `emon.tiffcheck` (`tc-check`, `tc-exif`) parse the container, decide accept or refuse by name (`emon.imgcheck`'s `ic-ok`, `ic-failed` = undecodable, `ic-unsupported`, `ic-limit`) and write what the host needs into a report `Cells` (`pr-*`, `tr-*`: size, displayed size, channels, resolution, orientation, bilevel; PNG: colour type, depth, whether the library carries alpha (`pr-alpha`) and whether samples are 16-bit (`pr-wide`): the D188 reduction; TIFF: samples, depth, compression, photometric, alpha kind, predictor, planar, fill order, byte order, tiles or strips, subsampling, the colour map and every chunk's offset and byte count already checked to lie in the file). `deep` 0 is the header answer (as an `info` request wants it). Both hosts read the whole input (a TIFF was read at random before; a multi-page TIFF still decodes only the frame asked for), call the validator, turn its status into `Fail`, and only then ask the library. **The library is shown `clean`**, a PNG the validator rebuilt from the chunks that matter, each copied as it was (IHDR, a palette image's PLTE, tRNS, IDAT, IEND): the animation chunks (acTL, fcTL, fdAT: a PNG's frame is its default image), a PLTE in a gray or true-colour image, and the ancillary chunks (gamma, ICC, text, time, eXIf, pHYs: read by kin) are not passed on. The pixel bound is `limit-of` PIXELS read inside kin (`imgdec::decode` and `imgDecode` lose their `max_pixels` argument; JPEG, which stays native, reads the same limit). Removed: Rust `png_sound`, `png_data_sound`, `png_raw_size`, `png_strip_apng`, `png_meta`, the CRC table, `Tf`/`Entry`/`Ifd`, `exif_of`'s reader, `dpi_rational`, `tiff_frame`'s tag reading (imgdec.rs 1364 -> 792 lines) and their Go twins (imgdec.go 1846 -> 1118); the host keeps the sample decompressors, the unpacking and the colour arithmetic.
**Why**: D396(4): a rule whose effect is observable is kin's, and two libraries' leniency must not be a difference between hosts. D389 had to patch it twice by hand.
**Alternatives**: validating on the library's side only (what D389 did); passing the original file and checking beside it (the library still reads chunks the validator did not judge: gamma, the palette in an RGBA image, which Go refuses and Rust reads).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D445 — What the PNG validator accepts, beyond D389 (P10.11; D389, D444)
**Decision**: D389's rules, now once, in kin, plus: tRNS once; a palette image needs its PLTE and has no more entries than `2^depth` (Go refused it, the Rust crate did not); colour type and depth must go together (0: 1 2 4 8 16, 2: 8 16, 3: 1 2 4 8, 4 and 6: 8 16), compression and filter method 0, interlace 0 or 1 (a header-only answer refuses them too: it used to give the size); the IDAT stream must END where the zlib stream does (a byte after it is refused; Rust ignored it); a PLTE in a type that does not use it is validated and dropped (Go refused it in an RGBA image). **Bytes**: the validator inflates the image data with `emon.inflate` into cells (four bytes a byte), so the inflated size the header implies is held to `limit-of` STREAM_BYTES (default 256 MiB) as well as the pixels to PIXELS: a PNG over it is `limit` with that count (the answer record names the pixels limit, as `rs-fail` breaches kind 9; naming STREAM_BYTES would change the transcript's answer, which is P10.9's/P10.10's). Memory for an accepted image is the inflated size x 4 until the check ends (`cells-free`). The kin inflate is bit-at-a-time (P10.3a is making it faster; it is called unchanged).
**Why**: one rule set; the cost of a second inflate pass is the price of D389's check, now paid in kin.
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D446 — What the TIFF validator accepts (P10.11; D188, D189)
**Decision**: the rules of the two hosts' readers, once: byte order and magic (BigTIFF 43 is `unsupported`); the chain of directories ends at a link of 0, one that does not lead to a readable directory, a directory seen twice (Floyd's two pointers: no table, no scan) or 2^20; a field is BYTE, SHORT or LONG, at most 2^24 values (64 for the samples), and its values lie in the file; all samples one depth of 1..16 bits; photometric 0 1 2 3 5 6 (others `unsupported`); a palette needs its map of `3 << bps` values; compression none, PackBits, LZW, Deflate (8, 32946), CCITT 3 and 4 (one-bit, one-sample), JPEG-in-TIFF and the rest `unsupported`; **CCITT Group 3 two-dimensional, uncompressed mode and fill bits stay `unsupported` as TIFF compressions** (`tiff-bilevel-g3-2d`, `-g3-fill` are refused by name in `expect.edn`; the decoder now reads them, and a law decodes both to the picture of the uncompressed file: changing the policy is an edit of `tc-frame` and of those two rows); predictor 1 or 2 (8 and 16 bits); planar YCbCr, float and signed samples `unsupported`. **New bounds** (a mutant could ask for them before): a tile may not be wider or taller than 2^20 nor have more pixels than the PIXELS limit (`limit`); the chunks the sizes need must be listed, with a byte count each (or the rest of the file for an image of one chunk) and every one inside the file; `deep` 0 does not read the strip tags at all, as before. EXIF (a JPEG's APP1, a PNG's eXIf) is `tc-exif` over the same reader, so the JPEG path keeps no TIFF code either.
**Why**: the check that used to happen lazily, strip by strip, in two idioms.
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D447 — One CCITT decoder, in kin, for TIFF and PDF; Go reads D337's Group 3 files (P10.11; D337, D189, D396(4))
**Decision**: `emon.ccitt` (`cc-decode data start end k cols rows flags out ws`) is T.4/T.6 written from the standard and from `pdfimg.rs`'s row loop (the code tables are `fax::maps`' = T.4's): Group 4, Group 3 one-dimensional and mixed, `EncodedByteAlign`, `EndOfLine`, fill bits, EOLs optional or required, EOFB and RTC. TIFF (`imgdec`) and PDF (`pdfimg`, the `decode-img` request) both call it, on both hosts; Rust's `fax` dependency (Cargo.toml in `emon-rs-build`/`emon-wasm-build`, Cargo.lock) and Go's `x/image` (go.mod, `host/go/go.sum`) are gone. **Contract**: the caller makes `out` hold `rows * stride` ZERO bytes (`vec![0; n]`, `make([]byte, n)`; a Java/C# host the same) and the decoder only sets black runs, so a page costs its transitions; a shorter `out` is status `cc-nospace`. A bad stream is `cc-bad` (a code in no table, a run past the width, a change element that does not move right, the data over before the rows, EOFB or RTC with rows owed, a row that needs an EOL and has none); `ws` is reused for every strip (tables built once, about 16 K cells). `K > 0` groups and byte-aligned or EOL-less Group 3 are read (they were Rust-only); the PDF path also holds `Columns * Rows` to the pixel bound. **Result**: `bb asset` is green with Go expecting the transcript's asset byte for byte for `ccitt-g3-1d-align`, `-noeol`, `-align-noeol` and `-g3-2d` (the four files that were `codec` on Go; `asset-check`'s special case and `engine_test.go`'s `codec` list lose them); `bb image` is exact on the 89 fixtures and its damage section holds G4 mutants to equal answers (the `fax`/`x/image` exemption is gone). **Speed** (scratch harness, release, Rust, equal work: kin `cc-decode` against `fax` painting the same packed rows; A4 at 300 dpi, one strip): text page G4 0.50x of fax's time, the same page as G3 1-D 0.34x, a noise page G4 0.91x, an almost blank page G4 (13 KB) 0.89x (the first version appended each row and was 3.3x on the blank page: the zeroed-`out` contract above is the fix). On main, `bb perf` (bet `ccitt`, P10.3) is the row: kin `cc-decode` against `fax` 0.2.7 `decode_g4` painting the same packed rows (`fax` is a dependency of `tools/perf` only, as a reference, and its encoder makes the streams), Group 4 at 2481x3508: the bench page (335 KB of G4) 1.06x of fax (median of 7 interleaved), a noise page (1.4 MB) 1.10x, a blank page (442 B) 1.23x; the quick synthetic text page 1.15x. The scratch ratios above (0.34-0.91x) did not repeat in this harness (different inputs and a different painting loop for `fax`; not investigated): kin is within 1.25x of `fax` everywhere, inside D092's 2x rule. Rows are in `tools/perf/baseline.edn` (quick and full). After the merge `bb unit` is 874 laws on Rust and Go (857 on main before).
**Why**: Go lacks Group 3 two-dimensional, Rust lacks alignment and EOL-less Group 3; neither is "adequate" (D396(4)).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

(The `bb perf` row for the CCITT decoder, listed here by the branch, was added at the merge: D447.)

### D449 — The Java host's native bindings use the Java FFM API (`java.lang.foreign`), not JNA or JNI; the floor is JDK 22 (P9.1; SPEC 13, 7.2; D007, D127, D211; the first branch's D520)
**Decision**: pdfium (`host/java/emon/ffi/Pdfium.java`) and Tesseract/Leptonica (`ffi/Tess.java`) are bound with the Foreign Function & Memory API, final since JDK 22 (here: 25). The libraries are found at RUN time (`EMON_PDFIUM_LIB`, `EMON_TESS_LIB`, the usual directories), so nothing links them and no gate needs them; a missing one is `emon.ffi.Unavailable`. pdfium's file-access callback is an upcall stub over the run's `RenderPort.Source`. The launcher `emon-java-build` writes passes `--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED`. ### D456 — The ImageDecode port in C#: kin decides and decodes PNG, TIFF containers, Deflate and CCITT; only JPEG stays native (P9.2; P10.11, D444-D448; D396(4), D187-D190; the first branch's D542)
**Decision**: `ImgDec` reads the whole file; `Pngcheck.PcCheck`, `Tiffcheck.TcCheck`/`TcExif` decide, report and bound it (D444-D446); CCITT G3/G4 is `Ccitt.CcDecode` (D447). The .NET BCL has no PNG codec (it has `System.IO.Compression`, which is DEFLATE and zlib only), so where Java hands ImageIO the validator's `clean` chunks, C# DECODES THE PNG IN KIN: the validator's joined IDAT payloads (`idat`) go through `Inflate.IzZlib` and the PNG filters of `pdffilter`'s `PfPng` (the code PDF's predictor uses; the generated method is assembly-internal, so no kin change), per Adam7 pass (the pass geometry is kin's `pc-adam`); what stays host code is the colour step (palette, `tRNS` colour key and per-entry alpha, 16 bits to 8 by `(v*255+32767)/65535`, sub-byte scaling, alpha over white, orientation): the arithmetic of Go's and Rust's decoders, D188. This costs a second inflate of the image data (the validator inflates once to judge it and frees the bytes). TIFF's strips and tiles are unpacked from the chunks the validator listed: LZW and PackBits are host code (the BCL has neither), Deflate is `Inflate.IzZlib` as well, with the three answers of the Rust host's `miniz_oxide` (a clean early end gives what it has, a stream that fills the strip has its end read so a wrong checksum is seen, one with more is cut) made from kin's status and its kept prefix; a stream bound breach inside a strip is that cut. **JPEG stays native (D190: lossy stays native; the BCL has no JPEG codec)**: the first host's decoder (baseline and progressive Huffman, Go's integer IDCT, libjpeg's fancy upsampling, now `Api/Jpeg.cs`, 715 lines) is kept and extended to four components for a PDF's CMYK/YCCK DCT (`PdfImg`). Deleted from the first host's `ImgDec` (3,031 lines, now 1,043 plus `Jpeg.cs`): its zlib (RFC 1950/1951), its PNG decoder, its TIFF container reader, EXIF reader and CCITT decoder. The BCL's `ZLibStream` is used in one place: `PngRead`, the transcript's own canonical PNGs (emon's file, not an input). A premise corrected: the BCL does have a zlib/DEFLATE stream; what it lacks is the PNG codec, and the choice of kin's inflate for untrusted input is for the answers (an exact status and a kept prefix instead of a stream's exceptions), not for want of one.
**Why**: one rule set (D444); D396(4): where the platform lacks a library, kin decodes. **Not done**: a PNG whose palette index is out of range is `failed` in all hosts that notice (Go, Java, C#); the JPEG decoders still forgive different damage (D448).
**Alternatives**: the first host's own PNG decoder (rejected: two PNG rule sets); `ZLibStream` for the PNG data and TIFF Deflate (rejected: its failures are exceptions of a stream, not the three answers).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D459 — The 33 `emon-live` regressions of `scan-color` and `scan-ovl`: they arrived with D391's merge (1e258e0), and they are five defects that the tilt fix made visible (D391, D393, D420)
**Decision**: bisection over `--first-parent`, in this worktree, with `bb accuracy --predictor emon-live --variants scan-ovl --ids invoice,bank-statement` (the two documents of `scan-ovl/forms`; local Tesseract 5.5.3, the committed synthetic corpus). The values of the entry were recorded by 639c610 (the P7.S merge; `git log -S` on the rows) and are reproduced there, at 5c7e490 and at f956211: `scan-ovl/forms` `block-table-f1` 0.25, `block-paragraph-f1` 0.4, `table-teds-lite` 0.056818. At **1e258e0** (D391-D394) they are 0.0, 0.25, 0.0, and stay so at 1729b31, 4336477, b2e4a8a and 175e2d8. The merge brings two commits and one change of `kin/`: b10d86c "deskew baselines by the page tilt" (`tb-tilt`, `tb-bkey` and the chain of `tb-rows`, `kin/table.kin`); b50259f is the guard and the DEVLOG. D391 measured the 71 `scan` documents, whose pages are tilted 0.7 degrees at most; the colour and overlay scans of the same documents are tilted up to 2.7 degrees (`scan-color/bank-statement` 2.72, -1.60, 0.62; `scan-ovl/bank-statement` 0.27, 2.38, 0.37; `scan-ovl/invoice` -0.93) and nobody had run `emon-live` over them after the merge. Nothing in the entry was an artefact (a pool or a gold change): D391 is RIGHT about the rows, and five things downstream of the rows had been tuned on rows that a tilted scan cut in halves. Per document:
 1. **`scan-ovl/invoice` loses its table** (`scan-ovl/forms` 13 and `scan-ovl/all` 8: block-paragraph, block-table, para-boundary, table-teds, table-continued-acc). The whitespace run of `tb-whitespace-page` is the header, the five items, the three totals and, 28.6 below (1.6 pitches), `Payment terms` and the two lines of the paragraph under it, which are rows of two chunks; `tb-score` refuses the run as a whole (text in cells, lowercase starts). Before D391 the tilt cut those rows in halves of one chunk, so the run happened to end at the totals. Nothing retried a shorter run.
 2. **A page header joins the table** (`scan-ovl/forms` bow-f1/p, ghost-rate; `scan-color/forms` paragraphs): `Account 40-22-18 / ... Statement 31 Mar 2026 | Page 2 of 3` is two chunks 40.3 above the header row of page 2 whose rows are 15.6 apart (2.6 pitches), and the run takes a row up to three times its size (41). The table then holds the line, `tb-claim` makes it a cell, and furniture cannot drop it: its words are ghosts (`ghost-rate` 0.154609 -> 0.165039).
 3. **Rows merged by a line's size** (`scan-color/graphics` 5, `scan-color/all` block-table-p): in `scan-color/mixed-table-image-shaded` the line `Reserve chen East 3,000` has `size` 26.15 (its box took in the printed band) among lines of 7.2-9.0; the chain tolerance is a third of the first word's size, 7.85 pt. The page's tilt (-10017 ppm) carries the right-hand words of a row 4.3 pt, the lines' own slopes are noise (+0.0017, -0.0083, 0.0000, 0.0000, -0.0122 against the page's -0.010), and the key gap between the third and the fourth row came to 7.45 pt: the two rows were one, and the table lost a row. The same size in `table-white-rules`' dark header band joined `nn en` to the first row.
 4. **A table's last column is also a note** (`scan-color/graphics` bow, ghost-rate): the column stage makes the narrow `Price 3.40 7.25 ...` of `gfx-shading-bands` a margin note (side fragment of four lines at most); once the table is found its cells are the same words, and `pa-notes` writes the note without asking `tb-claimed`: every price twice.
 5. **The fragments of a ledger on tilted pages do not join** (`scan-color/forms` block-table-f1/p 0.285714 -> 0.25): the boundaries of the columns of the three pages of `bank-statement` differ by the pages' tilts (2.7, -1.6, 0.6 degrees over 600 pt), `tb-same-columns` allows a sixtieth of the width, so a ledger of one table is three (gold: two tables, the key-value one and the ledger).
Fixed by D460-D464; D465 says what is still below the entry and why.
**Why**: the entry rows are the maintainer's committed values; D391-D395 hunted `scan`, and D420 measured the three variants for the first time since.
**Alternatives**: lowering the 33 values (they are not artefacts, above); undoing D391 (`scan/forms` CER 0.0502 against 0.1098, `scan-ovl/bank-statement` columns right, `table-multipage-*` whole).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D460 — A row of a tilted scan is told by its LINE: one key for every word of a line, the page's tilt carried from the line's start, and a chain tolerance of two sizes (`tb-bkey`, `tb-chain-tol`; D391)
**Decision**: `tb-bkey` (D391) carried each word's own right baseline point to the left edge along the page's tilt. A word's point is on its line's fitted baseline, so its key is `a + (s_line - s_page) x`: the slope noise of a short line (a pixel over 270 pt is 0.004) times the distance from the origin, up to 4 pt in a table 430 pt wide. Now the key of every word of a line is the line's START carried along the page's tilt (the first word of the line, found by `hd-line` at most 64 words back; a word with no line has its own point), so a line is one key and two lines of one visual row (Tesseract cuts a row at a wide gap) still meet, as D391 needed, to the error of the baseline at one point. The chain of `tb-rows` joins a word to the row when it is within a third of the first word's size AND of the smaller of its own and the previous word's size (`tb-chain-tol`): a line whose box took in a band is a large size and must not let the line below join its row. Both change only what has a size or a tilt of its own: a text layer (tilt 0, one size on a baseline) is as it was, `bb accuracy` emon 3246 metrics none moved.
**Why**: measured on `mixed-table-image-shaded` (D459 3): keys of a row spread 2.9 pt by word, 0 by line.
**Alternatives**: a per-word slope (D391's: noise); the lines' own slopes for the whole row (extrapolating a short line to the page's edge: worse).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D461 — A whitespace run is cut at what stands apart from it, and a run that is refused is tried without its tail (`tb-whitespace-run`; D459 1, 2)
**Decision**: `tb-whitespace-page` gives each run (rows of two chunks and the single-chunk rows between them) to `tb-whitespace-run` after cutting at its ends every row that is more than TWICE THE RUN'S MEDIAN PITCH from its neighbour (a page's running header above a table, a label under it). `tb-whitespace-run` drops rows of one chunk at either end and tries the rows; when `tb-score` refuses them, or the first or last row is a line of prose (`tb-prose-edge`: one cell of nine words or more, or every cell of two words or more beginning with a lowercase letter; tables of four rows or more) it tries again without that row, as long as three rows of two chunks are left and no more rows have been let go than are kept (a run of newspaper columns that is refused is not a table with some prose after it: `pdf/columns-newspaper` found a table of its three headlines when this had no limit). Laws: `test-a-tail-that-spoils-a-whitespace-run-is-let-go`, `test-a-running-header-apart-from-a-whitespace-run-is-no-row-of-it`, `test-the-rows-of-a-tilted-scan-are-told-apart-by-their-lines` (`kin/tabletest.kin`; all three fail on 71d5571's `kin/table.kin`).
**Why**: D459 1 and 2; the born-digital corpus is as it was (3246 metrics, none moved; `bb fusion`, `bb identity`).
**Alternatives**: the pitch cut inside a run too (tried: a ledger's key-value block above it became paragraphs and `heading-level-*` fell); a looser run builder (3 times the size is the run's own rule since P5.1).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D462 — The fragments of a table on two pages join when their columns agree to a twentieth of the width (`tb-same-columns`; D459 5)
**Decision**: the tolerance of the boundaries was a sixtieth of the table's width (at least 5 pt); it is a twentieth (at least 10 pt). On a scan each page has its own tilt, a column's boundary found over 600 pt of rows moves by the tilt (2.7 degrees is 28 pt) and the pages of `bank-statement` never agreed. The other conditions of P5.4 are as they were (the same number of columns, three or more; the first the last body block of its page and the second the first of its page; a repeated header row text for text; no caption of its own).
**Why**: `scan-color/forms` block-table-f1 0.25 (4 tables predicted, one right) -> 0.571429 (3 predicted, two right: `bank-statement` 3 tables -> the gold's 2); the born-digital corpus did not move.
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D466 — The seals regression of P8.3 was `emon.sigpx` reading the ink over a table's or a stamp's rule as a pen; four tests of the zone and of the ink, in kin (P8.3, D430; D419, D465)
**Decision**: `emon-live` `block-seal-f1`/`-p` fell in `scan/all`, `scan/seals`, `scan-color/all`, `scan-color/seals` and `scan-ovl/all` (and `scan/seals` `bow-p` was the P8.2 trade-off, D419) because the raster signature stage (D430) made a false `signature` or `initials` `seal` node of some two dozen zones of the three scan variants (every document converted live, one at a time, before and after): `scan`: `table-simple-ruled` (4), `table-slanted-header` (5), `mixed-two-tables` (3), `script-mixed` (2), `script-arabic`, `table-multipage-thead`, `stamp-seal` (the `PAID` stamp, 36 pt above a `Signed:` line) and `h-inverted` (initials); `scan-color`: `seal-over-text` (the table under the `PAID` stamp), `table-white-rules`; `scan-ovl`: `invoice`. A false node costs twice: it is a block that is not in the gold, and `sp-drop-lines` takes the OCR lines inside its box (words under 600 per mille) out of the body, which is where the table cells and rows went (`scan-color/all` `block-table-r`, `heading-p`, the `conf-*` rows of the tables). Four changes in `kin/sigpx.kin`, none to `emon.sigmark` or `emon.sealmark` (their vector path is not the scans'): (1) `sp-framed`: a vertical rule of at least 10 pt that meets the rule's row at its ends OR BETWEEN them is a cell border (was: at least 20 pt, at an end); a rule on the same line that ends where this one begins, or begins where it ends (6 pt, 4 pt of height), is the next cell of a row, and a long flat line (a scan's skew thickens a rule's box: 1 in 20) up to 28 pt above this rule's width or more is a row line above; (2) `sp-mask-words`: a word the engine was sure of (500 per mille) with at least two letters OR DIGITS is paper (was: two letters): the numbers of a table are not a pen (a lone digit still is: `ovl-sig-over-name` reads the first stroke as `4`, 737, and `bb sealpx` holds that box); (3) `sp-judge`: the pen is ON its line: the ink's foot is within 16 pt (`sp-gap`) or 40 per cent of its height of the rule, whichever is more (a stamp above a signature line is no signature; a signature crosses its line); (4) the signature fixtures are the contract that nothing is lost: `bb sigs` 3 of 3 signatures, 2 of 2 initials, 3 of 3 digital-signature fields, no body word lost, `bb sealpx` and `bb seals` unchanged, and `emon-sigs`/`emon-sealpx` hold their entries.
**Why**: the pen's tests (stroke width, loops, coverage) are true of a table's borders and digits and of a stamp's frame; what a signature has that they do not is a line of its own (nothing ruled above it, no cell beside it, no border across it) with the ink on it.
**Not built / open**: `scan/script-arabic` and `scan/script-mixed` are clean only because their table rows abut or stack; a table with no vertical borders, one rule and cells that are far apart is still a signature (the tracer breaks a rule at a stamp: D419's page). The thresholds are first values (P10.1). `table-multipage-thead` was not recorded with its pixels (the recorder hung on it, 30 minutes at no CPU; the live run of it converts); its false signature is gone in the live run.

### D471 — The C binding is the Rust host behind `host/c/include/emon.h`: the browser binding's ABI, in C types, with explicit memory, categories and names for errors, and a boundary no panic crosses (P9.4; D001, D058, D356-D361)
**Decision**: `host/c/src/capi.rs` is assembled into the Rust crate by `kin/scripts/emon-bind-build lib` (the same assembly as `emon-rs-build`: the generated modules and `host/rust/src/`, a `lib.rs` that is the host's plus the line `pub mod capi;`, so **`host/rust` is not changed**) and built as a `cdylib`, a `staticlib` and the `rlib` the pod links. `host/c/include/emon.h` is the header and the documentation. Two ways in, the two the Rust host has. **One-shot**: `emon_convert`, `emon_convert_json`, `emon_convert_html`, `emon_intake` take an `emon_input`: bytes (copied) or a **lazy `emon_source`** (a `length` and a `read_at(ctx, offset, buf, len)` callback, pread's contract: SPEC 13.1, D058/D074/D075; the engine reads only the spans it touches, in chunks of the options' `chunk`: 14370 of 40482 bytes in 29 reads for `h-plain` at 512) and a password; with `EMON_NATIVE` the call uses the library's own pdfium, Tesseract and OpenJPEG/jbig2dec when it was built with them (`EMON_RS_PDFIUM`, `EMON_RS_LIVE`, `EMON_RS_CODECS`, the switches of `emon-rs-build`; `emon_capabilities()` says which). **Inverted**: `emon_open` .. `emon_step` .. `emon_finish` with `emon_prefetch`, `emon_provide`, `emon_fail`, `emon_answer`, `emon_answer_ocr`, `emon_bitmap_png`, `emon_ocr_*`, `emon_replay_file/_end`, `emon_transcript`: `host/wasm/src/wasm.rs`'s ABI one for one (status 0 done / 1 need bytes / 2 need requests, the unit that missed re-run inside `emon_step`), with C types (`emon_range` of two u64, `emon_request` records pointing into one cell pool) instead of an output buffer. **Options are kin's text** (`emon.config`: `key=value` lines; `emon_check_options`, `emon_is_option_key`; a bad text is kin's sentence), the same grammar as the drivers and the browser; `record=1` and `js-ocr=1` are a session's and a one-shot refuses them. **Memory**: emon allocates, the caller frees with `emon_free_buf/_error/_model/_step/_files/_asset_info`; pointers passed in are borrowed for the call (`emon_provide` and an input's bytes are copied); an `emon_buf` has a NUL after `len` (JSON and HTML are C strings); a free clears its struct and is safe to repeat. **Errors**: a function answers `0` (or a status) or `-code` and fills the `emon_error` it is given: `code` is the category (one per kind of the host's `Error`, D040's, 13 of them, `EMON_ERR_*`; `emon_error_category` names them), `name` is the stable name to route on (kin's: a PDF status, a limit such as `input-bytes`, a plan error such as `transcript-miss`), `message` the sentence. **Panics are caught at every entry point**: a panic is `internal` with its message (`emon_test_panic` shows it); the engine works on a **worker thread with a 32 MiB stack** so a caller's 256 KiB thread is nothing the answer depends on (the C test runs a conversion on one); a handle is for one thread at a time. The `input-bytes` bound is checked against `length` **before** the chunk cache is allocated (the browser binding allocates first: a chunk of 1 and a 2 GiB length would ask for gigabytes).
**Why**: the browser binding's ABI is already what a binding needs (D001 says the C binding sits over the Rust host), so the C one is that ABI with pointers, plus what C needs and a browser does not: ownership, a stable header, a lazy source it can implement with `pread`, and a boundary that survives a bug.
**Alternatives**: one global output buffer like wasm.rs's (not thread-safe, and a C caller wants to keep results); handles as integers in a table (a pointer is C's idiom); a callback-driven `render/ocr` registration for the step API (the caller of the step API fulfils by answering, which is what the browser does); error codes per kin name (kin's names are open-ended: a PDF status is a string; the category is the number, the name the string).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D472 — What the C binding gives and does not: the Model as JSON/HTML/assets, not its walk; the caller fulfils `ocr` only; the session logic is wasm.rs's, copied (P9.4)
**Decision**: the C binding gives SPEC 13's `convert`, `intake`, `record` and `replay` (the last two as a session with `record=1` and a replayed transcript, which records and replays **the very directory the Rust host writes**, byte for byte: `bb identity`), an input that is bytes or a lazy source with a password, and the Model **as its interchange forms**: `emon_model_json`, `emon_model_html` (the drivers' `--html=` list, external assets with a prefix), the evidence dump, and the assets (`emon_model_asset_count/_info/_bytes`: name, media type, origin, sha256, size). **It does not give `Model.root()`, `pages()`, `find()` and the node walk** of SPEC 3.9: a C caller reads the JSON (the format SPEC 4 defines, with a parser in every language), and a second tree API in C is a second thing to keep identical. Like the browser binding, **the step API's caller fulfils `ocr` (with `js-ocr=1`) and nothing else**: `render` and `crop` are answered `unsupported` by the session, `decode`/`decode-img` by emon from the bytes provided (a caller that renders passes the one-shot `EMON_NATIVE` instead); the codecs of `decode-img` (JPX, JBIG2) are the one-shot's too. The session logic (`Session`, `step`) is `wasm.rs`'s **copied, not shared**: factoring it into a host file both bindings include would change `host/rust` and the wasm build, which the browser arm of `bb identity` (not run where there is no wasm toolchain) must then re-prove. It is the open item for P9.5.
**Why**: the maintainer's list for P9.4 is the one-shot call, the step API, option text, errors and assets; the walk is a Rust/Go/Java/C# idiom (`Node` borrows the Model) that no binding over a C ABI can give without owning a second object model. Copying keeps `host/rust` untouched, as the task required.
**Alternatives**: a C `emon_node_*` API (rejected, above); host/rust refactored into a shared `Stepper` (right, and P9.5's).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D473 — The C test program, the C driver and the arms: a C compiler is the only extra, and without one every arm skips loudly (P9.4)
**Decision**: `host/c/test/emon_test.c` (59 checks, from the repository root) is the C test: the goldens through the one-shot and the step API, a lazy source and its failures (`io`, `source-changed`), the named errors by category and name, kin's option text, assets, record and replay, every free, a panic that does not cross, a 256 KiB thread; `kin/scripts/emon-c-build` compiles it, **against the shared library and against `libemon.a`** (so the static one needs nothing a C program does not have), and the C driver `test/driver/c/emon-c.c`, the twin of the Rust driver (same flags, stdout and exit codes; `--source=bytes|seek|spool|step`, `--async`, `--record/--replay`, `--native`), with the system C compiler (`CC`, else `cc`, `clang`, `gcc`; `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`). **Without a compiler it prints `SKIP c -- why` on stderr and exits 3, and every caller leaves the arm out and says so** (`EMON_SKIP_C=1` leaves it out on purpose). `bb c` builds and runs the test, holds `emon.h` to the built library's exports (42 functions, exactly), and runs the driver's four ways in. `bb slice` runs the C test (both libraries) and the C driver through every section the other hosts have (goldens, async 512, the adapters, evidence, errors, passwords, assets). `bb identity` has the C driver's **five arms** (one-shot over bytes, over a lazy pread source, over a spooled stream, the step API, the step API over 512-byte chunks) and its record/replay trip (records Rust's directory, replays Rust's, Rust replays its). `bb embedders` holds the header to the Rust file, SPEC 13's verbs and the browser's exports (each has its C counterpart).
**Why**: the same shape as the Java and C# arms (D449, D457): a toolchain that is not there is a loud skip, never a pass and never a failure.
**Alternatives**: the C test as a cargo test calling the `extern "C"` functions (it would not prove the header, the ABI, or a C compiler's reading of either).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D474 — The pod is a Rust binary over the Rust host that adds no crate: bencode, EDN, JSON-to-EDN and base64 are written in it (P9.4)
**Decision**: the route is **a Rust binary (`host/pod/src/main.rs`, `emon-pod`) linked to the same assembled library** (`emon-bind-build pod`), speaking the pod protocol (bencode over stdin/stdout, `format` EDN). The alternatives and why not: *(a) the pod over the C binding* (Rust calling its own C ABI) adds a layer that does nothing, since the pod can call `Engine` directly; *(b) a pod in Clojure on the JVM* is a fifth host (D001: bindings add no kin arm) with a JVM start-up per `bb` run, and bb has no FFI to reach the C library; *(c) a Go pod over the Go host* is a second binding over a different host, against D001. **No crate is added**: bencode (50 lines), an EDN reader and writer for the pod's data, JSON-to-EDN for the Model, and base64 are written in the file, so the pins are the Rust host's (`host/rust/Cargo.lock`, unchanged: `image =0.25.10`, `miniz_oxide =0.8.9`, `zune-jpeg =0.5.15`, `zune-core =0.5.3`); the wire is small enough to be read in one sitting. **The ops** (namespace `emon`, loaded by `babashka.pods/load-pod`): `emon/convert INPUT [OPTIONS [SPEC]]` where INPUT is a path (a **lazy** `Read + Seek` source: the engine reads chunks as it touches them) or `{:path | :bytes <base64>, :password}`, OPTIONS is kin's text, and SPEC says what to return (`:model` `:json | :json-pretty | :edn`, `:html` true or the drivers' list or a vector of lists, `:evidence`, `:assets :bytes | :info`, `:native`; a vector asks for a vector) and defaults to `{:model :json :html true :assets :bytes}`; it returns `{:model :html :evidence :assets :intake :stats}` in **one call and one conversion**; `emon/intake`, `emon/check-options`, `emon/option-key?`, `emon/capabilities`. Errors are exceptions: the engine's sentence and `ex-data {:name :code :category}` (the name is kin's, the code the C binding's category). The Model as EDN is the JSON's data (a name that reads back as a keyword is one, a number is a number): the pod test reads the JSON with cheshire and requires equality. Bytes cross as **base64** because a pod carries EDN, not byte arrays. Known edge: a top-level `false` reaches babashka as `nil` (`emon/option-key?` is truthy/falsey; inside a map a `false` is `false`).
**Why**: the simplest route that is a real pod; the shortest wire that carries what the task names (a path or bytes plus option text in, the Model as JSON or EDN plus HTML and the assets out); no dependency to pin or to keep.
**Alternatives**: `serde_json`/`bencode` crates (more to pin for 300 lines we would still have to test); returning the Model only as JSON (the maintainer asked for EDN too); a stateful pod with model handles (the C binding has them; babashka has no way to free one, so the pod returns data).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D475 — The pod's test, its driver and its arms: the pod converts in one call, so it has no async source and no transcript (P9.4)
**Decision**: `bb pod` (`kin/scripts/pod`) loads the pod with `babashka.pods/load-pod` and converts the slice's seven fixtures **by path and by base64 bytes** to the goldens (`test/para/NAME.json`, `test/slice/NAME.html`, `NAME.full.html`) in one call each, requires the Model as EDN to be the JSON's data, `chunk=512` to give the same Model (29 reads of the path), the errors by name and code (D040's, the limit's by its name, `usage` with kin's sentence), a password to open the locked file to the plain twin's Model, the assets of `dct-rgb.pdf` (the JPEG, its bytes, size and sha256), the evidence golden, images, and the four small ops (58 checks). `test/driver/pod/emon-pod` is the pod's driver, the twin of the Rust driver's CLI, a babashka script that loads the pod named by `EMON_POD` (`kin/scripts/emon-pod-build` writes a one-line launcher `.cache/emon-pod/emon-pod`); `bb slice` runs it through every section of the other hosts, **except** that the pod has no async source, so `--chunk=512` stands in for `--chunk=512 --async`; `bb identity` has **two pod arms** (path, base64 bytes) over the whole corpus and the three asset passes, and leaves the pod out of an input that replays a committed transcript and of the `--full` async arms (a pod has no transcript to replay and no miss to re-run). **Without babashka on the PATH or with `EMON_SKIP_POD=1` it skips loudly** (exit 3, `SKIP pod -- why`); the pod needs nothing else.
**Why**: byte-identical to the Rust driver on the slice and the identity set is the same claim every host makes; what a binding structurally cannot do (replay, async) is not asked of it.
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D476 — The build: one assembled crate for both bindings, `cdylib` + `staticlib` + `rlib` + `emon-pod`, the same switches for native ports, no new dependency (P9.4)
**Decision**: `kin/scripts/emon-bind-build lib|pod` assembles `.cache/emon-bind` (or `.cache/emon-bind-live` when `EMON_RS_LIVE=1`, `EMON_RS_PDFIUM=DIR` or `EMON_RS_CODECS=DIR` is set, so the plain and the native builds do not rebuild each other) with `Cargo.toml` `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib", "staticlib", "rlib"]` and `[[bin]] emon-pod`, the dependencies of `emon-rs-build` verbatim and `host/rust/Cargo.lock` as its lock file: **no crate is added and no pin changes**. `capi.rs` exposes four plain-Rust helpers the pod shares (`category_code`, `category_name`, `html_options`, `native_config`) so the two bindings report the same categories and take the same html list. Verified live on this machine with the pinned pdfium, Tesseract 5 and OpenJPEG/jbig2dec: for `h-plain.pdf` (born-digital, `ocr=always`) the C one-shot with `EMON_NATIVE` gives the Rust driver's `--pdfium --tesseract --codecs` bundle byte for byte and the pod with `:native true` gives its JSON byte for byte (a native build is shared-only: its static library would need the native libraries on the link line).
**Why**: one build, one lock file, the bindings being the Rust host (D001).
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D1120 — The step session is one module, `host/rust/src/session.rs`, that `wasm.rs` and `capi.rs` both call: not kin, because it is host state over `engine::Run` (D396, D472)
**Decision**: the inverted API's state machine -- `Session` (open, prefetch, provide, fail, replay_file/_end, step, answer, answer_ocr, bitmap_png, transcript, finish, finish_intake) with its round logic over `engine::Run` and `plan::Machine`, the `Fault` (engine error or `usage`) both bindings map errors from, the input-bytes check, and the stateless helpers both exported (`constant` = `emon_const`, `parse_html`, the four `ocr_*` policy calls, `intake_line`, `panic_message`) -- lives in `host/rust/src/session.rs`, declared `pub mod session;` in `lib.rs` and copied by `emon-rs-build`, `emon-wasm-build` and `emon-bind-build`. **Each binding keeps only its ABI**: `wasm.rs` the linear-memory pointers, the one output buffer (`put_*`), the handle table and the exports; `capi.rs` the `emon.h` shapes, explicit frees, `guarded` (the panic catch), the 32 MiB `on_worker` thread, the `emon_step_out` cell pool. The Session is never given a thread: the C binding calls it on its worker, as it called its own copy. The crate root re-exports nothing from it (the embedders' surface is unchanged); `emon.h` and the wasm exports are untouched, so `host/js` is too. A pure move: `bb identity` and the C/pod/ocr arms are byte-identical (see D1121 for the one change). **Home**: a module in `host/rust`, not kin (D396 says kin by default). The logic is not observable in the sense kin's laws are: it is state held across calls of an ABI (a `Run` with its arenas, a `ChunkCache` the caller pushes into, a boxed port closure, a `Replayer`), and every decision in it that IS policy is already kin's and called from it (`pl-route`, `pl-spans`, `ox-flat`, `op-*`, the plan `Machine`); what remains is the order of Rust calls over host types that kin has no model of. Putting it in kin would mean a kin model of `Run` to move the same calls into, which is the Rust host written twice.
**Why**: D472 copied `wasm.rs`'s session into `capi.rs` to leave `host/rust` untouched for P9.4, and said so as the open item: two copies of a state machine are the drift D396 says to avoid (a fix to a round in one is a bug in the other, as the input-bytes check already was).
**Alternatives**: `capi.rs` including `wasm.rs` by `#[path]` (couples the C binding to a browser file, and the wasm one has no `Fault`); a kin session model (above); a trait the bindings implement for output (the outputs are two return values, `Step`; a trait is more than they need).
**Result**: `capi.rs` 1219 -> 958 lines and `wasm.rs` 777 -> 519 lines (together 1996 -> 1477, with `session.rs`'s 410 the one copy: 1887 in all); `parse_html`, the `emon_const` table, the panic message and the intake line are written once.
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)

### D1121 — The `input-bytes` bound is checked before the chunk cache is allocated in the browser binding too: the C binding's check moves into the shared `Session::open` (D471, D1120)
**Decision**: `Session::open` refuses a length over the `input-bytes` limit (the options' limit, at most `i32::MAX`) as `Error::Limit { input-bytes, limit, actual }` BEFORE `ChunkCache::pushed` allocates the chunks' table. The C binding had this (D471: "the browser binding allocates first: a chunk of 1 and a 2 GiB length would ask for gigabytes"); the browser binding now has it, because it is the same call. This is a FIX, the only behaviour change of the move. What a caller sees: the same error name and category (`limit`, `input-bytes`) as before; `actual` is now the real length (capped at `i64::MAX`) where the browser binding's engine check reported the stand-in `2^31` for any length that did not fit an `i32`; a length over a lowered limit (`limits=input-bytes=N`) is refused here, not one step later. Nothing else in `open` changed: the chunk is still `65536` for 0 in the browser and the options' `chunk` in C, passed by each binding. The engine's own check in `start_pushed` stays (a native `Run` has no `open`). The change is kept to the one `if`, since the limits work (P10.4) may touch limit checks.
**Why**: a check that guards an allocation belongs before it, and a fix found in one copy belongs in both.
- [ ] **Signed off** (maintainer)
